I'm sorry about your dad. I can help you three talk this through; I can't make legal decisions or move money. Before any plan, I want to understand needs rather than argue positions.

You mentioned A and her husband buying at a "family discount," not signing off on that, and B being able to use some money. For each of those: what matters to you, and why does it matter? What matters to you about the house and your dad's will? What are you worried might get brushed aside, even as a small discomfort?

I'll summarize what I hear as a positive "what you want" statement, with no specific outcome in it, and record it only after you say the wording fits. Silence won't count as agreement, and you're welcome to say no or change any wording.

What matters to me is a fair financial share. I haven’t agreed to subsidize A’s discounted purchase. I need to know what B using money would mean for everyone before I can say how I feel about that. I want the will and house handled fairly, and my silence shouldn’t count as consent. Your principle about freely confirmed understanding fits.

DRAFT OPTIONS — for validation only, not a decision, not settled. I make no legal decision and move no money; any qualified professional would only explain the will or handle documents if you choose to instruct them. Each is drafted to meet every confirmed NCE, and none assumes a specific outcome:
Option 1, shared facts and a pause: each of you explicitly, in your own words, agrees to pause any sale, discount, price, terms or distribution; a qualified probate/legal professional explains what the will actually allows; an independent valuation gives a baseline; plain numbers then show how any arrangement the will allows would affect each sister's share. A's possible purchase with her husband, B's studio hope, and your fair share all stay on the table. Nothing is signed, no terms are assumed, and your explicit agreement is required before anything affecting your share.
Option 2, purchase by A only on explicitly agreed terms: after Option 1's facts, A and her husband may propose a purchase, with any price or terms — including or excluding a discount — discussed only after the effect on every share is visible and only with your explicit agreement. B's studio hope is taken seriously in considering how any proceeds are used within what the will allows; A's independence and wish to buy are not dismissed; all three may take independent advice, say no, and re-check this list before any documents are considered. If any of you says no, no purchase on those terms proceeds; the no is added as a need.
Option 3, all legally available alternatives, chosen only by explicit agreement: after the same shared facts, a neutral professional lays out the arrangements the will actually allows (for example, holding the house, a purchase, a third-party sale, or distribution) with the effect on each share; each sister explains at her own pace what matters to her; B's hope is not framed as taking from her sisters, A's wish to buy is not set aside without her say-so, and your share and clear agreement are required. You all re-check the list, add any new concerns, and only then say whether any arrangement meets every confirmed need. If none does, that is an acceptable outcome for now, recorded as unresolved.

How I weighed them against the list: all three require qualified legal input, an independent valuation, explicit confirmation, room for small doubts and no pressure; all keep your fair share, effects-first and nothing-settled concerns, A's independence and undecided terms, and B's studio hope with unpressured room to speak.
